description_full: Moog Inc. designs, manufactures, and integrates precision motion and fluid controls and controls systems for original equipment manufacturers and end users in the aerospace, defense, and industrial markets in the United States, Germany, and internationally. The company operates through four segments: Space and Defense, Military Aircraft, Commercial Aircraft, and Industrial. Its Space and Defense segment provides critical defense components and motion-control systems used in defense vehicle platforms, missile systems, naval ships and submarines; high-performance components and systems used for space launch vehicles, satellites and spacecraft vehicles. The Military Aircraft segment designs, manufacture and integrate primary and secondary flight controls, mission-critical actuation systems, and products for various military fixed-wing aircraft and rotorcraft for both original equipment manufacturers and aftermarket customers. The Commercial Aircraft segment designs, manufactures, and integrates flight-critical control systems and products for various commercial aircraft including widebody, narrowbody, business jets and regional jets. The company's Industrial segment provides customized and high-performance motion control components and systems for industrial automation, medical, simulation, and test and energy applications, including precision components used in heavy machinery, medical devices and components, power generation products, as well as simulation platforms for flight training and material testing applications. The company was formerly known as Moog Valve Company. Moog Inc. was incorporated in 1951 and is headquartered in East Aurora, New York.

financial_summary: Moog Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $10.2B market cap on $3.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 29%.

The business throws off $128M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.16× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.6× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.2×.
Shareholder yield is only 1.7%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 12% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.06x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+3.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 89% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 25% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 28% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 38% and a beta of 1.02, it moves roughly with the market.
About $96.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 63% in the 2020 crash, 21% in the 2022 bear market and 62% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $166 (margin of safety -95%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 44%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $99.31 to $268 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: EV/EBITDA 17.2 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 79.8 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 119% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $445 on average, 38% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 9.5%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.15).
It runs a 29% gross margin and converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.16x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.4% of revenue on R&D and 0.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.6x net debt to EBITDA ($62.0M of cash against $945.7M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.2x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.0, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.3% over 3 years, 6.0% over 5 years and 4.3% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 44% of profits supports about 5.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -7.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.25 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.6x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 24%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.4x, 3.7% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 9, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.8%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (15 sales, net $3.2M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.7% (1.4% in buybacks and 0.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 13,500 employees, each generates about $286K of revenue, 0.8x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 4.1% a year.
That works out to $10K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (9x revenue per employee).
